name: The Purkinje Effect
statement: As light fades to dusk, reds darken and blues brighten as the eye shifts to its rods.
meaning: The Purkinje effect, or Purkinje shift, is the tendency of the eye's peak sensitivity to brightness to move toward the blue end of the spectrum as light levels fall. In bright light, the eye is most sensitive to yellow-green wavelengths and reds appear relatively bright and vivid; but as light dims toward twilight, red objects appear to darken faster while blue and green objects appear relatively brighter, so a red flower and a blue flower that look equally bright in daylight will have the blue one look brighter at dusk. This shift accompanies the transition from cone-based daytime vision to rod-based night vision. It is named after the Czech anatomist and physiologist Jan Evangelista Purkyně, who described it around 1819 after noticing that flowers bright red in afternoon sun looked very dark at dawn. The Purkinje effect explains a range of everyday observations about colour at twilight and underlies the use of red light to preserve night vision.
mechanism: The human retina has two kinds of photoreceptors with different roles. Cones handle bright-light, or photopic, vision and colour, and are collectively most sensitive to wavelengths around five hundred fifty-five nanometres, in the yellow-green. Rods handle dim-light, or scotopic, vision, do not signal colour, and are most sensitive to shorter wavelengths around five hundred to five hundred seven nanometres, in the blue-green, and are essentially insensitive to long-wavelength red light. In bright light, cone vision dominates and reds look bright. As light dims and vision shifts toward the rods, the overall peak of brightness sensitivity moves toward the blue end, because the rods respond better to shorter wavelengths and hardly at all to red. So reds fade to dark while blues and greens hold their brightness or appear relatively brighter, producing the Purkinje shift. The effect follows directly from the differing sensitivity curves of the rod and cone pigments and the handover from cone-dominated to rod-dominated vision as illumination decreases.

examples.text: A red flower that looks bright in daylight turns dark at dusk, while blue and green flowers appear relatively brighter as vision shifts to the rods.
Bright-light cone vision peaks in the yellow-green, but dim-light rod vision peaks in the blue-green and is blind to red, shifting sensitivity blueward.
Astronomers, submariners, and pilots use red light because it barely stimulates the rods, preserving dark adaptation while cones handle reading.

variants.name: Photopic and scotopic peaks
variants.text: The cone peak near five hundred fifty-five nanometres in bright light versus the rod peak near five hundred to five hundred seven nanometres in dim light.

variants.name: Red-light night vision
variants.text: The practical use of red illumination to preserve rod dark adaptation, an application of the rods' insensitivity to red.

whyItMatters: The Purkinje effect is a classic and instructive phenomenon in vision science, revealing the two-system structure of human vision and how it changes with light level. By showing that the eye's peak brightness sensitivity shifts toward blue as light dims, it demonstrates the handover from cone-based colour vision in bright light to rod-based vision at night, and it explains a range of everyday experiences of how colours look at twilight, when reds go dark and blues seem to glow. The effect has a well-known practical application: because the rods that provide night vision are insensitive to red light, red illumination is used where dark adaptation must be preserved, in astronomical observatories, submarines, aircraft cockpits, and darkrooms, letting people see by red light without spoiling their night vision. Understanding the Purkinje effect thus connects the physiology of rods and cones to the design of lighting and to the perception of colour under changing conditions. As Jan Purkyně's early-nineteenth-century observation, it remains a foundational demonstration of how vision adapts to light.

limits: The Purkinje effect describes the shift of brightness sensitivity across the transition from cone to rod vision, so it appears specifically at low, twilight light levels where both systems contribute or vision is becoming rod-dominated, not in full daylight or full darkness. The exact peak sensitivities of rods and cones are approximate and vary somewhat, and the shift depends on the wavelengths and the state of dark adaptation. Because rods do not signal colour, deep scotopic vision is essentially colourless, so the effect concerns relative brightness rather than a change in hue perception at the lowest light. The practical red-light application works because rods are insensitive to red, but red light still allows cone-based reading.
misreadings: The Purkinje effect is not that objects change colour at dusk; rods do not signal colour, so it is a shift in relative brightness, with reds darkening and blues brightening. It does not occur in full daylight or total darkness, but during the twilight transition from cone to rod vision. And red light preserves night vision not because it is dim but because the rods are insensitive to red, so treating the effect as a hue change, as happening at all light levels, or red light as merely dim, misreads a blueward shift of brightness sensitivity tied to the cone-to-rod handover.
origin: Named after the Czech anatomist and physiologist Jan Evangelista Purkyně, who described it around 1819; the shift of peak brightness sensitivity toward blue in dim light as vision moves from cones to rods.
